clue.text: Lurid coverage of something very juicy?

definitions.text: Lurid coverage of something very juicy?

parts.words: Lurid coverage of something very juicy?
parts.note: surface reading: sensational press reports about a scandalous story
setter's reading: a glaringly bright-coloured skin wrapped round a juicy fruit

explanation.surface: A tabloid splashes a scandal across its pages in lurid detail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lurid' and 'juicy' both sound like gossip journalism, but here lurid is literal: vividly coloured, as the rind of a citrus fruit is.
explanation.definitionFit: The rind of this citrus fruit is bright in colour and encloses flesh full of juice, so it is literally a vivid wrapping.

indicators.note: the actor famously slurs his s sounds into sh, so a word is to be heard in his accent

parts.note: a bureau is an office, which in a Connery accent comes out with a sh ending

explanation.surface: A remark that the Bond actor's office has a stylish, cool look.
explanation.walkthrough: Sean Connery, the Scottish actor who played James Bond, is widely imitated saying 'sh' for 's', so 'office' becomes this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone offish is aloof and distant in manner, which is the chilly sense of cool rather than fashionable.

clue.text: American poet getting in round on ship?

parts.note: A is a standard abbreviation for American

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a bard is a poet
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: An American poet climbs onto a boat, the question mark asking if he is really on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'on ship' is only one example of the answer's meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Being aboard means being on or in a vessel or vehicle, and a ship is the classic example of this.

clue.text: Get away from London? Many PMs do this

definitions.meaning: first meaning: leave the city for the countryside
second meaning: a prime minister calls a general election

explanation.walkthrough: In British politics a prime minister (PM) who calls a general election is said to take the question to the voters of the whole nation.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally means a trip to rural parts, and idiomatically means dissolving parliament and asking the electorate to vote.

clue.text: With great speed, present glue to Spooner

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the words are to be said his way

parts.note: to present a show is to host it; its opening sound is swapped with the next word's
glue is paste; its opening sound is swapped with the previous word's

explanation.surface: An instruction to hand over some glue to Spooner as fast as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like the verb 'give', but it is host, as in presenting a programme.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb comes from the old urgent mail carriers, meaning very quickly, with all possible haste.

clue.text: English vehicle heading to Stewart Lee, comedian

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a van is a vehicle

indicators.note: a heading sits at the top, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: An English car goes to fetch the comedian Stewart Lee.
explanation.walkthrough: Stewart Lee is a real comedian, so the reader groups 'Stewart Lee' together; the split falls between the two names, and Lee Evans is another British comedian.
explanation.definitionFit: Lee Evans is a well-known British stand-up comic, so his surname fits the description of Lee the comedian.

indicators.note: something reported is spoken about, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: to bend down low to avoid something is to duck

explanation.surface: A plumber is told that a pipe has been bent out of shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' looks like an adjective for the pipe, but it is a past-tense verb for bobbing down.
explanation.definitionFit: A duct is a tube or channel carrying air, liquid or cables, essentially a kind of pipe.

indicators.note: to engineer is to construct or contrive, so the letters are built into something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: People protest furiously because an engineer has spoiled a map.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' reads as the person ruining the map, but it is a verb telling you to rebuild the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes people who are indignant and loudly objecting, as if they had taken up weapons.

indicators.note: something mobile moves about freely, so the letters shift position

parts.note: taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A phone lies beneath an elderly comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beano is a long-running British children's comic magazine, home of Dennis the Menace; 'comic' looks like a comedian but means the magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beano is a weekly publication of cartoon strips, which is what the British call a comic.

parts.note: George Best was a famous Northern Irish footballer, so Best prompts his first name
Harrison Ford is the film actor, so Ford prompts his first name

explanation.surface: Asks which Ford car is the best one for a musician to drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' and 'Ford' look like an adjective and a car maker, but both are surnames of famous people whose first names are wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: George Harrison was the lead guitarist of the Beatles, so he was a celebrated musician.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an outward appearance put on for others
second meaning: the forward end of a ship

explanation.walkthrough: The pair reads like a stage direction to take a bow; each word is a separate sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A front is a pretended outward display, and it is also the foremost part of a vessel, which sailors call the bow.

clue.text: Maybe Python Cleese finally takes little drink

parts.note: a python is one kind of snake, as 'Maybe' signals
a little is a bit

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of the surname

explanation.surface: John Cleese of Monty Python at last has a small drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Python' with 'Cleese' conjures Monty Python, but here it is the snake, an example flagged by 'Maybe'.
explanation.definitionFit: A snakebite is a British pub drink of lager mixed with cider, so it is a kind of alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Graze from rodent caught in school

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, so the pieces before it sit within the one after

parts.note: SCH is the abbreviation for school
a rat is a rodent
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A child gets a graze from a rat trapped in the school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught in' reads as one phrase, but caught is C, from cricket scoring, and only 'in' places the pieces. SCH is a standard abbreviation for school.
explanation.definitionFit: A graze is a light wound where skin is scraped, which is the same injury as a scratch.

clue.text: 5 Down for example, flipping geezer drilling safe

indicators.note: a drill bores into something, so one piece goes into the middle of another

parts.note: a safe bet is a sure one

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: geezer is British slang for a man

explanation.surface: A safecracker, described with the mild British oath 'flipping', drills into a safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British oath before 'geezer', but it tells you to reverse. 5 Down is EVANS, which is a family name.
explanation.definitionFit: Evans is a family name, so it is an example of the category of names passed down in families.

parts.note: reports are news
the Tate is the London art gallery, with its possessive
a piece in chess or draughts is a man

explanation.surface: A magazine runs reports on an artwork in a gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the group of national art galleries in London; a chess piece is traditionally called a man.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Statesman is a long-running British weekly of politics and culture, so it is a periodical publication.

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
thick is British slang for stupid
to deserve something is to earn it

explanation.surface: Someone answers stupidly and largely deserves to be punished for it.
explanation.walkthrough: A thick ear is British slang for a swollen ear from being hit, as in 'you'll get a thick ear'.
explanation.definitionFit: A thick ear is a cuff round the head given as a rebuke, an old-fashioned informal physical punishment.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: communicates with someone by phone or message
second meaning: lenses worn on the eye to correct sight

explanation.walkthrough: 'Visual aids' sounds like charts in a presentation, but it means lenses that aid vision.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach someone by phone is a verb sense, and lenses worn directly on the eyeball are the plural noun sense.

parts.note: prime means of the top quality
an outstanding debt is one still owed

explanation.surface: Receiving the top Amazon subscription service is described as excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise but means unpaid; 'Prime' looks like a name but means top quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bestowed has been conferred or presented as a gift or honour, so it has been given.

clue.text: Where inaccurate lobbed pass could go, too hard

definitions.text: Where inaccurate lobbed pass could go
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ball thrown too high sails above the receiver

explanation.surface: A sports commentator notes a wayward high pass that was too hard to control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too hard' reads as describing the pass's force, but it is a separate meaning: too difficult to understand.
explanation.definitionFit: A badly aimed high ball literally goes above a player, and a concept that is too difficult figuratively goes beyond comprehension.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a person claiming to contact spirits
second meaning: a means of communication

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive makes it read as a psychic's television channel; the two words are separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiritualist who relays messages from the dead is one sense, and a means by which something is conveyed is the other.

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold within one's arms, so the answer is held inside the words

parts.note: the letters sit across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone finds fault with a counsellor who is hugging a copy of scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Embracing' seems to be the therapist holding the Bible, but it tells you the letters are held by the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is one of the books of the Old Testament, telling of a Jewish queen of Persia.

indicators.note: to model is to shape or mould, so the letters are formed into something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A huge model is stored up in the loft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giant model' reads as a big replica, but 'model' is a verb telling you to reshape the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective the word means enormous or colossal, from the Titans of Greek myth, matching giant used adjectivally.

clue.text: Snack cold in middle of brasserie

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
in, meaning fashionable, is hip

indicators.note: the middle is the centre point, so only the central letter is wanted

parts.note: the fifth of nine letters

explanation.surface: A cold snack is served in the middle of a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a linking preposition, but it is the adjective meaning trendy.
explanation.definitionFit: Chips, fried potato pieces or crisps, are commonly eaten as a light bite between meals.

parts.note: 'Oh brother!' and 'Cor!' are both exclamations of surprise
to take home pay after deductions is to net it

explanation.surface: A brother carries some musical instruments back to his house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cor' is a British exclamation of surprise, as is 'Brother!'; 'takes home' is earnings after tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornets are small brass instruments like trumpets, common in brass bands, so they are musical instruments.

clue.text: Quality of chicken, farm animal I cared about

parts.note: a cow is a farm animal

indicators.note: about can mean around or all over the place, so the letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A farmer describes the qualities of a chicken and of another animal they looked after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' sits among farm animals but is slang for a coward.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone chicken means they are fearful, so the quality of a chicken in that slang sense is lack of bravery.

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
W is the abbreviation for wife
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A man's stylish second wife is attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word after the definition is a standard single-letter abbreviation except 'is', which stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Swish is informal British for smart and fashionable, a close synonym of stylish or elegant.

indicators.note: going back means going in the opposite direction, so the letters are read from right to left
a set number of letters found within, so a run of that length sits inside the next word

parts.note: four consecutive letters inside the word

explanation.surface: A football pundit discusses the defensive back four of Sweden's national team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back four' is a football defence line, which fits the team; here it tells you to read four letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A side is a sports team, as in the home side or the national side.

clue.text: "Maestro possibly bored by performing with Queen" — Mercury expert?

indicators.note: something bored has a hole drilled into it, so one piece is pushed inside another
possibly suggests one arrangement among several, so the letters may be reordered

parts.note: taken as written
a performer on stage is on
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A review of a maestro performing with the rock band Queen, whose singer was Freddie Mercury.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen and Mercury conjure Freddie Mercury, but Mercury is the planet and Queen is R, for Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who studies the planets and stars would be a specialist on the planet closest to the sun.
